One of the responsibilities of any chosen generation is not only to create new technology -- innovations that will make life's burden lighter for those who follow -- but also to show how such power should be used wisely.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

How did my parents navigate their world?

It was simpler in many ways, yet they faced questions as profound as ours.

What guided their decisions?  How did they know when they were right — or when they were off the mark?

Their knowledge came not from textbooks but from experience. Life itself was their classroom. They learned through hardship, through relationships, and through observing the consequences of choice. The lessons they passed down were not theories, but living truths — offered to spare us the pain of repeating their mistakes.

They warned us of visible dangers: debt, addiction, reckless habits. But they also guarded us from the invisible ones — apathy, pride, and the loss of gratitude.

![](images/IMG_1883%20(2025-11-05T22_44_32.506)~2%20Copy.JPG)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Then, one born in 1949, addresses a generation shaped by digital light and neural networks.

His topic: **Deep Learning in the Age of AI**.

I wondered if someone in his mid-seventies could truly grasp and address the complexities of artificial intelligence — how to benefit from technology without being consumed by it.

I was wrong.

He understood our challenges more clearly than most and offered an elegant, time-tested solution.

He began by acknowledging his hosts with grace, then turned to the young audience and said:

“It’s a great season in the Lord’s work… You are those children… The Lord is preparing wonderful opportunities for you to experience deep learning, but they come with important challenges.”

He then introduced the Elements of Deep Learning: Know. Feel. Do. Become.

And he illustrated them through the Principle of Repentance — to know truth in the mind, to feel it in the heart, to act upon it in righteousness, and to become more like the Savior.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Two thousand years ago, the Apostle Paul wrote:

“Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.” (2 Timothy 3:7)

Or, as rendered in classical Chinese (和合本)[^1]:

[^1]: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Union_Version?oldformat=true>

常常學習，終久不能明白真道

“Constantly studying and practicing, yet never able to clearly understand the true Way.”

Thank you, Professor Kim B. Clark[^2], for reminding us that true learning — whether in faith or technology — must engage the whole soul: the mind, the heart, and the spirit -- centered on Christ or the Way.

[^2]: <https://www.linkedin.com/in/kim-b-clark-19664920a/>
